big: Rohan is offered a ₹30 lakh home loan with a smiling line: 'Your EMI is only ₹26,992.' Nobody mentions that over twenty years he will hand back about ₹64.8 lakh.

lines: The EMI fits my salary, so the loan is fine, right?
The EMI is the smallest, friendliest number. Ask for the total you will repay, and what the loan really costs.

note: Early on, most of each EMI is interest, since you still owe almost everything.

alt: Two sets of bars comparing EMI and total interest for a short and a long loan
caps: Same loan, same rate, two tenures.
Fifteen years: EMI about ₹30,400 a month.
Twenty-five years: EMI about ₹25,200 a month.
That ₹5,200 saved each month costs about ₹20 lakh more in interest.

q: A lender quotes Meena only the EMI of her loan. Which number should she ask for as well?
opts: The lender's profit made in the last year
The total she will repay over the whole loan
The EMI of a loan that her friend took
The number of branches the lender has
why: The lender's yearly profit says nothing about what her own loan costs her.
EMI times months, less the principal, shows the true price of the loan.
A friend's EMI depends on other terms, so it will not show her cost.
Branch numbers do not tell her what she will repay in total.

q: Rohan stretches his loan from 15 to 25 years to get a smaller EMI. What is the trade-off?
opts: A lower EMI, and less interest paid overall
A higher EMI, but he finishes the loan sooner
No change in cost, since the rate stays the same
A lower EMI, but far more interest over the years
why: Interest rises with tenure, so the total cost goes up and not down.
A longer tenure lowers the EMI, so this describes the opposite choice.
The rate may stay the same, but the longer time means a bigger total cost.
A longer tenure cuts the monthly burden but adds many years of interest.

q: Why is most of the first EMI interest?
opts: Interest runs on the balance, highest at the start
Lenders always take interest first as a fixed rule
The principal is paid off before any interest starts
Early EMIs are always bigger than the later ones in the loan
why: Interest runs on what is owed, and early on almost the whole loan is owed.
It is not a rule of taking interest first. It follows from the large balance.
Principal and interest are mixed in each EMI from the first month.
A standard EMI is the same amount each month for the whole tenure.

q: Meena takes home ₹80,000 a month. Which total of EMIs follows the 40% guide?
opts: Any amount, if the lender approves
why: ₹60,000 is three quarters of her pay, far above a safe share.
₹72,000 is nine tenths of her pay and leaves almost nothing for life.
Forty percent of ₹80,000 is ₹32,000, which leaves room if a month goes wrong.
Lender approval is a limit on the lender's side, not a safe level for her.

pts: Ask for the total repaid, not only the EMI.
A longer tenure lowers the EMI but raises the interest by a lot.
Keep all EMIs together under about 40% of take-home pay.
